newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi Arabia sets out privatisation goals.
newsitem.headline: Saudi Arabia sets out privatisation goals.

text.p: Saudi Arabia has spelled out its privatisation plans, saying it aims to increase the competitiveness of local industry, lure foreign capital and cut state spending, while providing more jobs for its 12 million nationals.

In its weekly meeting late on Monday, the cabinet chaired by King Fahd said the kingdom was committed to giving the private sector a bigger role in the world's largest oil producer and exporter, the official Saudi Press Agency (SPA) reported.
But the cabinet gave no details on which state firms or functions it planned to privatise, nor did it indicate when the long-discussed process might be launched.

The key goals of the plan include: encouraging national and foreign capital to invest locally; increasing job opportunities and raising per capita income; increasing the effectiveness of the Saudi economy and its ability to face world competition "especially in light of joining the World Trade Organisation".
Saudi Arabia hopes to join the world trade body by 2002.
The cabinet plan also aimed to provide services "at the appropriate time and cost", SPA said.
Many basic services -- from water and electricity to air travel -- are heavily subsidised in the desert kingdom, fuelling high government budget deficits since the early 1980s.
The plan spoke of cutting state spending and "alleviating the government's budget burden by allowing the private sector to finance, operate and maintain some services it can carry out".
In the past few years Saudi Arabia has said it wants to freeze new government capital spending and get the private sector to finance new infrastructure development.
But contractors say they are unwilling to fund projects, like water and power plants, that do not generate profits.
The cabinet plan aims to increase state income "from the returns of participation in the activities of the private sector and the sale of its assets".
The kingdom has said it plans to sell off its national carrier Saudi Arabian Airlines, but economists say that until it earns profits, investors will stay away.
They say top of the list of privatisation candidates is 70 percent state-owned Saudi Basic Industries Corp.
The plan said Saudi Arabia should "gradually select" those firms or functions to be privatised. But it came with a caveat.

"Upon the selection of various activities being transferred to the private sector it should be taken into consideration economic growth, the government's budget, national workforce, low income people, and the participation of a large tranche of naitonals in this activity."
The cabinet statement also said it planned to "preserve the role of the government in providing essential services and social welfare to the nationals."
